summary: Describes the IS-IS extensions needed to run Segment Routing over the IPv6 data plane. Segment Routing encodes a path as a list of segments, and this document lets IS-IS advertise the information routers need for that on IPv6. It updates RFC 7370 by modifying a registry.

eli5.summary: A trip is written as a list of stops, and each stop is an IPv6 address. IS-IS is how routers tell each other which stops exist.

questions: what is the srv6 locator tlv
what is an srv6 end sid
subtitle: How IS-IS routers tell each other about SRv6 segments: locators, SIDs, behaviors and hardware limits.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) steers packets through a list of instructions called segments, but IS-IS had no way to advertise the locators, segment identifiers and behaviors that routers need to build such paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a new SRv6 Locator TLV, an SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV, End SID, End.X SID and LAN End.X SID sub-TLVs, an optional SID Structure sub-sub-TLV and new Maximum SID Depth types.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS can now carry everything a router needs to advertise SRv6 support and its SIDs. The RFC also updates RFC 7370 by modifying an existing IANA registry.

today: RFC 9352 is a Proposed Standard from February 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 7370 by modifying an existing registry.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needs SRv6 Extensions
sections.content:
With Segment Routing (SR), a node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments. Segments are identified by Segment Identifiers (SIDs). SR can run directly on the IPv6 data plane using the Segment Routing Header, and that combination is called SRv6.

This document specifies the IS-IS extensions that let the protocol encode SIDs and the behaviors bound to them. The RFC assumes the reader knows the SRv6 network programming model from RFC 8986. In short, it adds a Locator TLV, a Capabilities sub-TLV, sub-TLVs for maximum SID depths, and three sub-TLVs that say which SIDs a node has and what Endpoint behavior each one has.
sections.eli5: Routers already use IS-IS to share maps. This RFC teaches IS-IS a few new words so routers can also share the list of stops a trip may use.

sections.title: Capabilities, Algorithms and Depth Limits
sections.content:
A node says it can act as an SR Segment Endpoint by advertising a new SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV (type 25) inside the Router Capability TLV. Its only defined flag is the O-flag: when set, the router supports the O-bit in the Segment Routing Header. All other bits are reserved, MUST be zero when sent and MUST be ignored when received.

Supported algorithms are advertised with the Segment Routing Algorithm sub-TLV from RFC 8667.

The RFC also defines four Maximum SID Depth (MSD) types, building on RFC 8491. They tell other routers how many SIDs a node can handle. If no value is advertised for any of them, the router is assumed to lack the ability (for Max Segments Left the supported value is 0).

An incorrect MSD advertisement may have negative consequences, because other routers may build paths the node cannot process.
sections.eli5: Each router raises a flag that says I understand these trips, and also says how long a list of stops it can handle at once.

sections.title: Locators, SIDs and Reachability
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID is 128 bits made of locator, function and argument parts. A node has a locator for each topology/algorithm pair it supports, and the locator is a covering prefix for all SIDs of that pair on the node. Locators MUST be advertised in the new SRv6 Locator TLV (type 27). Receivers MUST install forwarding entries for them when they support the topology/algorithm, using the same process as Prefix Reachability TLVs 236 and 237.

Locators for algorithms 0 and 1 SHOULD also be advertised in TLV 236 or 237 so that legacy routers install a forwarding entry. If the same prefix shows up in both, the Prefix Reachability advertisement MUST be preferred. Flexible Algorithm locators SHOULD NOT be advertised in those TLVs, as that would make them follow the algorithm 0 path.

SIDs learned from other nodes are not directly routable and MUST NOT be installed in the forwarding plane. They are reachable only through a covering locator, which must be the longest match prefix for them.

Section 6 adds an anycast flag (bit 4, the A-flag) to the Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV. All nodes advertising the same anycast locator MUST instantiate the exact same set of SIDs under it, or traffic may be dropped or misrouted. The A-flag and the N-flag MUST NOT both be set.
sections.eli5: A locator is like a street name that covers every house on it. Routers learn the street first, and only then can they find a particular house number (a SID).

sections.title: The Locator TLV and SID Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The SRv6 Locator TLV (type 27) holds a Multi-Topology Identifier and one or more locator entries. Each entry has a 4-octet metric, a flags octet (with the D up/down bit), a 1-octet algorithm, a 1-octet Loc-Size (1 to 128 bits; the whole TLV MUST be ignored if it is outside this range), the locator itself in 1 to 16 octets, and optional sub-TLVs. The Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV SHOULD be included, and MUST be included when the entry is leaked upwards or redistributed.

The SRv6 End SID sub-TLV (type 5) lives inside the Locator TLV and advertises SIDs whose behavior needs no particular neighbor. It carries a flags octet (none defined), a 2-octet Endpoint Behavior, the 16-octet SID and optional sub-sub-TLVs. The SID MUST be allocated from its locator, or it is ignored.

SIDs tied to a neighbor use the SRv6 End.X SID sub-TLV (type 43, point-to-point) and the SRv6 LAN End.X SID sub-TLV (type 44, which adds the neighbor System-ID). Their flags are B (eligible for protection), S (refers to a set of adjacencies) and P (persistently allocated), plus a 1-octet weight for load balancing. Such SIDs MUST be a subnet of a locator with matching topology and algorithm from the same node.

The optional SID Structure sub-sub-TLV (type 1) gives the lengths in bits of the locator block, locator node, function and arguments. The four lengths MUST add up to at most 128 bits, and it MUST NOT be used at a transit node for forwarding.
sections.eli5: These are the forms routers fill in. One form lists a street and the houses on it. Other forms list doors that lead to one particular neighbor.

sections.title: Which Behaviors Go Where
sections.content:
Endpoint behaviors and their codepoints come from the registry in RFC 8986. This RFC says which sub-TLV each may appear in. A behavior MUST only be advertised in the TLVs marked Y and MUST NOT be advertised in those marked N. Not every behavior from RFC 8986 is covered; End.T, for example, is not.

Behaviors that need no specific neighbor, such as End and the End.DT forms, go in the End SID sub-TLV. Behaviors that forward to a neighbor, such as End.X, End.DX6 and End.DX4, go in the End.X and LAN End.X sub-TLVs. A receiver ignores behavior values it does not support or recognize.
sections.eli5: Some jobs are done at the router itself, and some jobs hand the packet to a neighbor. The RFC says which form to use for which kind of job.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the SRv6 Locator TLV (27) in the IS-IS top-level TLV registry, the SRv6 End SID sub-TLV (5), the SRv6 Capabilities sub-TLV (25), the End.X and LAN End.X sub-TLVs (43 and 44), and the MSD types 41, 42, 44 and 45. It also adds the A-flag as bit 4 of the Prefix Attribute Flags registry.

New registries are created for sub-sub-TLVs of the Capabilities sub-TLV, sub-sub-TLVs of the SRv6 SID sub-TLVs, and flags of the Capabilities sub-TLV, the Locator TLV, the End SID sub-TLV and the adjacency SID sub-TLVs. Registration in them is by Expert Review. The existing registry from RFC 7370 for sub-TLVs of prefix reachability TLVs is updated with a column for the Locator TLV, which is why this RFC updates RFC 7370.
sections.eli5: Every new word needs an official number in a shared dictionary, so two vendors never use the same number for different things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns for IS-IS are covered in ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. IS-IS usually runs inside a single administrative domain, but where attackers may reach the routing domain, the stronger authentication mechanisms in those documents SHOULD be used.

The security considerations of SR (RFC 8402) and of SRv6 network programming (RFC 8986) apply too. The RFC also points to RFC 8491 for the harm an incorrect MSD value can cause, to RFC 9259 for the O-flag, and to RFC 9350 for Flexible Algorithm.
sections.eli5: If a bad actor could whisper false directions to the routers, trips would go wrong. So routers should check who is talking to them.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: No flags defined; all bits reserved.

fields.name: Endpoint Behavior
fields.desc: Behavior code from the RFC 8986 registry.

fields.name: Sub-sub-TLV-len
fields.desc: Octets used by the optional sub-sub-TLVs.

items.label: SRH Max Segments Left
items.desc: Maximum Segments Left value in a received SRH before applying the Endpoint behavior.

items.label: SRH Max End Pop
items.desc: Maximum number of SIDs in the SRH for which PSP or USP can be applied.

items.label: SRH Max H.encaps
items.desc: Maximum number of SIDs that H.Encaps can add to the segment list.

items.label: SRH Max End D
items.desc: Maximum number of SIDs in an SRH when decapsulating.
